overview.text: Ralph Ellison’s novel *Invisible Man* (1952) is a first-person coming-of-age story narrated by an unnamed Black man who describes himself as invisible because society refuses to recognize him. His journey from the South to New York and Harlem exposes racism and the pressures of institutions and political movements that try to define him. Encounters with a paint factory and the Brotherhood, an organization claiming to help oppressed people, mix social critique with surreal and sometimes comic episodes. His underground refuge frames an ongoing search for identity and self-determination. Recognized as an important work of American literature, the novel explores African American life amid unequal treatment; Ellison became the first Black author to win the National Book Award, in 1953.

key_facts.text: The novel was published by Random House in 1952.
Its unnamed narrator’s invisibility is social and metaphorical: people fail to recognize or pay attention to him.
The narrator’s journey takes him from the South to New York City and Harlem.
He lives in an underground room illuminated by 1,369 stolen lightbulbs.
Ellison won the 1953 National Book Award for the novel, becoming the first Black author to receive the award.
